sections.skill: Tell deductive conclusions from inductive ones

questions.prompt: Which argument is a valid DEDUCTIVE argument (its conclusion must be true whenever its premises are true)?

choices.text: Every swan I have seen is white. So all swans are white.
Every prime number greater than 2 is odd. 31 is a prime number greater than 2. So 31 is odd.
Most students like recess. So Ana likes recess.
The last 20 buses were on time. So the next bus will be on time.

questions.correct_answer: Every prime number greater than 2 is odd. 31 is a prime number greater than 2. So 31 is odd.

questions.prompt: "1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16. So the sum of the first n odd numbers is always n x n." What kind of reasoning is this?

choices.text: deductive: the examples prove it for every n
neither: it is not an argument
inductive: it generalizes from a few examples

questions.correct_answer: inductive: it generalizes from a few examples

questions.prompt: In an inductive argument, the premises can all be true while the conclusion is false.
questions.correct_answer: True

questions.prompt: n x n + n + 11 is prime for n = 1, 2, 3, ..., 9. A student concludes it is prime for every whole number n. Which value of n shows the conclusion is false?
Which conclusion follows DEDUCTIVELY from "All members of the chess club are in grade 10 or grade 11, and Jun is a member of the chess club"?

choices.text: Jun is in grade 10 or grade 11.
Most grade 10 students are in the chess club.

questions.correct_answer: Jun is in grade 10 or grade 11.

sections.relationship: Classifying reasoning needs the premises and the conclusion to be identified first.
sections.author_note: Classifying reasoning needs the premises and the conclusion to be identified first.

questions.prompt: "All the cookies are gone, so someone ate them." Which part is the conclusion?
questions.correct_answer: someone ate them

questions.prompt: A premise is the statement that an argument is trying to prove.
questions.correct_answer: False

questions.prompt: "It rained every day this week. So it will rain tomorrow." What is the premise?

choices.text: It rained every day this week.

questions.correct_answer: It rained every day this week.

questions.prompt: Every argument has at least one premise and one conclusion.
questions.correct_answer: True

questions.prompt: "Since 12 is even, 12 is divisible by 2." What is the conclusion?
questions.correct_answer: 12 is divisible by 2

sections.relationship: Deduction aims to make the conclusion certain; induction only makes it likely. Students need to judge certainty first.
sections.author_note: Deduction aims to make the conclusion certain; induction only makes it likely. Students need to judge certainty first.

questions.prompt: "The sun has risen every morning on record, so it will rise tomorrow" has a conclusion that is certain, not just likely.
questions.correct_answer: False

questions.prompt: "Most tickets in the box are red, and I drew a ticket" makes "my ticket is red" certain.
questions.correct_answer: False

questions.prompt: Which word signals that a conclusion is only likely?
questions.correct_answer: probably

questions.prompt: If a pattern holds for 100 examples, it must hold for the 101st.
questions.correct_answer: False

questions.prompt: A die has been rolled 5 times and showed an even number each time. Which conclusion is certain?

choices.text: The next roll will be even.
Each of those 5 rolls was even.
The die only has even numbers.

questions.correct_answer: Each of those 5 rolls was even.

sections.relationship: Harder: test generalizations that hold for many cases and then fail.
sections.label: ADVANCED APPLICATION

questions.prompt: The claim "n x n - n + 17 is prime for every whole number n" holds for n = 1 to 16. Find a whole number n that makes n x n - n + 17 NOT prime.
questions.rule: (not isPrime(n*n - n + 17) and n >= 1 and isInteger(n)) and isInteger(n) and n >= 0
questions.correct_answer: any values that satisfy: (not isPrime(n*n - n + 17) and n >= 1 and isInteger(n)) and isInteger(n) and n >= 0 (example: n = 17)

questions.prompt: Points are placed on a circle and every pair is joined by a straight line. With 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 points (in general position), the circle is cut into 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 regions. A student predicts 32 regions for 6 points. What is the actual number?
A valid deductive argument with true premises can have a false conclusion.
questions.correct_answer: False

questions.prompt: Which statement is the strongest inductive argument?

choices.text: All bolts in the batch passed, so this bolt passed.
My two friends like the song, so everyone does.
The first bolt passed, so all bolts pass.
All 500 randomly chosen bolts from the batch passed, so nearly all bolts in the batch pass.

questions.correct_answer: All 500 randomly chosen bolts from the batch passed, so nearly all bolts in the batch pass.

questions.prompt: Which reasoning is deductive?

choices.text: Most rectangles in the book are squares, so this one is.
All squares are rectangles; this figure is a square; so it is a rectangle.
Every rectangle I measured had equal diagonals, so all rectangles do.
This figure looks like a rectangle, so it probably is one.

questions.correct_answer: All squares are rectangles; this figure is a square; so it is a rectangle.

sections.relationship: Expert: tell when a pattern has been proved and find the exact failure point.
sections.label: EXPERT CHALLENGE

questions.prompt: The expression n x n + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, 2, ..., 39. What is the smallest whole number n for which it is NOT prime?
"For every whole number n, n x n - n is even, because 2 x 2 - 2 = 2, 3 x 3 - 3 = 6 and 4 x 4 - 4 = 12 are even." Which statement about this argument is correct?

choices.text: The claim is true, but three examples do not prove it.
The claim is false, because 1 x 1 - 1 = 0.
The argument proves the claim, because three cases are checked.
The claim is false for large n.

questions.correct_answer: The claim is true, but three examples do not prove it.

questions.prompt: If every case of a finite list has been checked, the conclusion about that list is deductive.
questions.correct_answer: True

questions.prompt: Give a whole number n from 1 to 20 for which "2 to the power n, minus 1, is prime" is FALSE, even though n is prime. (2 to the power n is 2 multiplied by itself n times.)
questions.rule: (isPrime(n) and not isPrime(2^n - 1) and n <= 20) and isInteger(n) and n >= 0
questions.correct_answer: any values that satisfy: (isPrime(n) and not isPrime(2^n - 1) and n <= 20) and isInteger(n) and n >= 0 (example: n = 11)

questions.prompt: A student checks that every whole number from 4 to 100 that is even can be written as a sum of two primes. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: Every even number greater than 2 is a sum of two primes.
Every even number is a sum of two primes.
Every even number from 4 to 100 is a sum of two primes.
No odd number is a sum of two primes.

questions.correct_answer: Every even number from 4 to 100 is a sum of two primes.
